title: The days of distress (Mark 13:14–27)
hook: strange apocalyptic images; Christians read them in several ways

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was little apocalypse, and your line was don't worry beforehand.

This part reads like a dream you can't explain the next morning. Still on the Mount of Olives, Jesus goes on. When you see a terrible thing standing where it shouldn't, run. On the roof? Don't go down for anything. In the field? Don't go back for your coat. Pray it doesn't happen in winter. Then the sky seems to come apart: sun darkened, moon gone dim, stars falling. Then Mark steps out of the story with an aside in parentheses, to you, the reader. In the King James Bible: "let him that readeth understand." Pay attention.
screen: `LIKE A DREAM YOU CAN'T EXPLAIN.` → `RUN. DON'T GO BACK.` → `LET HIM THAT READETH UNDERSTAND.`

segments.voice: The terrible thing is called the abomination of desolation, a phrase from the book of Daniel. The first book of Maccabees uses it for a real event: under a foreign king, Antiochus, a pagan altar was set up in the temple. The temple's rededication after that is what Hanukkah remembers. The sun darkened, the moon not giving her light: Isaiah used pictures like these for the fall of Babylon. Then they'll see the Son of man coming in the clouds with great power and glory, another picture from Daniel, and he'll gather his chosen from the four winds. What does it mean? Christians land in different places. Many read the coming in the clouds as Christ's return at the end of time, which the Nicene Creed confesses: he shall come again. Some read nearly all of it as already fulfilled when Rome destroyed the temple. Others read it as still ahead, a future time of trouble. Some also read a rapture here, alongside Paul's line about believers "caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air": the faithful taken away before the trouble. That reading spread widely from the 1800s on, and many evangelical churches teach it; Catholic, Orthodox and many other Protestant churches don't. If you grew up afraid of coming home to an empty house, know that it is one reading among several. Mark doesn't settle it. He warns against people with confident timelines, and later in this speech gives a promise: "Heaven and earth shall pass away: but my words shall not pass away." Whatever the images mean, those words are offered as the steady thing.
screen: `DANIEL'S ABOMINATION OF DESOLATION.` · `A SKY COMING APART.` · `THE SON OF MAN IN THE CLOUDS.` · `SEVERAL READINGS, ONE PROMISE.` · then, large: `MY WORDS SHALL NOT PASS AWAY.`

segments.voice: Take one line as the steady thing: heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away. Breathe in on the first half, out on the second, and if frightening pictures come, from this chapter, the news or your own worries, come back to the line. If you pray, rest your fear in that promise.
Maccabees, the book that records a real desecration of the temple, the abomination Jesus borrows as a phrase for a new disaster.
Your line: my words won't pass away. Whatever shakes, that promise stays. Day two hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Christians confess in the Nicene Creed that Christ "will come again"; churches read this chapter especially in Advent, and interpret its images in several ways, from the fall of the temple to Christ's return at the end of time.

fork.setup: you're a first reader of Mark. you hear of the abomination of desolation standing where it ought not. what does the text tell you to do?
options: flee to the mountains and don't go back.
fork.reveal: flee: from the roof, from the field, don't go back even for a coat. and don't trust anyone with a confident timeline.

original.note: Greek: an abomination, something detestable. from Daniel's phrase, the abomination of desolation.

trapdoor: what you thought: a map of the end of the world.
what it means: dream-like pictures of disaster, read in several ways, held together by a promise that his words won't pass away.
what a scholar hears: Daniel's abomination, used in 1 Maccabees 1:54 for Antiochus's altar; cosmic imagery from Isaiah 13:10; Mark's own aside to the reader.

notes: Rewritten 2026-10-06 from the five-year map; confirm with the Keeper. Added an early, light rapture beat (research: a real childhood fear of being 'left behind'); the fuller treatment stays in year 4 (day 1316). Confirm: the pre-tribulation rapture reading spread from the 1800s (J. N. Darby, later the Scofield Bible), taught by many evangelical churches and not by Catholic, Orthodox or many other Protestant churches. Tone check: no fear used as a teaching device. To make room, the line 'Some read the first part as about the Roman war' was cut (the 'already fulfilled when Rome destroyed the temple' reading stays), and the myth about 1 Maccabees was swapped for one on the rapture.

Editor review (2026-10-01): Cut "Mark does something he never does anywhere else" (unsourced superlative); "brackets" now "parentheses" as in the KJV. Removed the dating of Daniel and "about two centuries before Jesus"; the Antiochus link now rests on 1 Maccabees (cited). "Israel's prophets ... the fall of empires" narrowed to Isaiah 13:10 and Babylon. The readings paragraph no longer uses "many scholars", "most Christians" or the year 70; the creed is named (Nicene). Myth, trapdoor and howItsDone aligned. Note for Keeper: 1 Maccabees is deuterocanonical for Catholic and Orthodox readers and Apocrypha for Protestants.

Readings summarized without ranking: preterist (fulfilled in 70), the majority expectation of Christ's return (creeds), futurist (a future tribulation), and the view that 13:14–23 concerns 70 while 24–27 concerns the end. Keeper to confirm fairness.

Antiochus IV's altar (167 BCE) and Hanukkah's rededication (1 Maccabees 4); 'about two centuries before Jesus'. Confirm.
'Mark does something he never does anywhere else': the parenthetical address to the reader in 13:14 is unique in Mark. Confirm.
